subtitle: Recognize prohibited practices, understand the reporting and review duties around emergency manual restraint, and examine person-centered supports. This course supports plan review; it does not qualify anyone to use restraint or replace required provider training.
audience: For case managers and care coordinators, lead agency staff, 245D provider oversight and licensing-adjacent staff, and DSD program, policy and supervisory staff who review support plans, incident reports or provider practices for people with disabilities.

lessons.title: Why Minnesota moved to positive supports
objectives: Identify which providers and settings the Positive Supports Rule applies to.
Explain the four purposes for which 245D prohibits restrictive procedures.
Describe the quality-of-life goals DHS names for the rule.
Compare a compliance-only reading of the rule with a quality-of-life reading.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota's Positive Supports Rule, Minnesota Rules chapter 9544, works together with Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D to govern how licensed providers respond to behavior that concerns them. The rule covers home and community-based services governed by chapter 245D for people with disabilities and people sixty-five and older. It also covers certain chapter 245A settings serving people with a developmental disability or related condition. DHS describes its purpose as improving quality of life for people, including children, who receive the covered services. It requires person-centered principles and positive support strategies.

The core prohibition sits in 245D. The statute lists chemical, mechanical and manual restraint, time out, seclusion and other aversive or deprivation procedures. Providers may not use them to replace adequate staffing, as punishment or for staff convenience. They also may not use them as a behavioral or therapeutic program to reduce or eliminate behavior. Use these four purposes to examine the stated reason and actual effect of a practice. Seek observable evidence rather than assuming a staff member’s motive. Other restrictions and requirements still apply; the absence of one prohibited purpose does not authorize a procedure.

DHS names several goals: community participation, inclusion in the most integrated setting and high-quality environments. Supports should be developed with the person and build skills, choice and quality of life. The goals also include freedom from humiliating treatment and an end to aversive and deprivation procedures, with consistent standards across settings. Notice that most of these are about what should be present in a person's life, not only what should be absent.

That difference shapes oversight. A compliance-only reading asks whether prohibited procedures were avoided and reports were filed on time. A quality-of-life reading also asks whether the person is doing more of what they enjoy, has more control and more relationships, and is less often in situations that lead to distress. Both readings matter. Formal licensing findings belong to DHS Licensing and its governing process. Staff reviewing a plan within their role can also ask quality-of-life questions. A report count does not establish whether incidents occurred, reporting was complete or supports were effective.
lessons.keyPoint: The Positive Supports Rule is about building a good life, not only avoiding forbidden procedures. Restrictive practices are prohibited as a substitute for staffing, as a behavior program, as punishment or for staff convenience.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Tamsin is a DSD program consultant reviewing provider quality data. One provider has had no restraint reports for a year and all paperwork on time. In site visit notes, however, she reads that residents are rarely out in the community, several people spend most evenings in their rooms, and staff describe a 'quiet house' as the goal. Another provider has filed several reports but shows steady growth in outings, jobs and friendships for the people it serves.
lessons.question: What should Tamsin do next?
choices: Treat the first provider as the model because it has no restraint reports.
Treat the second provider as the concern because it files more reports.
Look beyond report counts and ask both providers how they measure and support quality of life, including community participation and choice.
feedback: An absence of reports does not establish an absence of incidents or a good quality of life. A quiet house can reflect restriction, low staffing or disengagement rather than good support.
More reports may reflect more incidents, more complete reporting or other differences that need examination. Report counts alone cannot tell you whether a provider is doing well or poorly.
This is the strongest response. It uses the rule's own quality-of-life goals as the measure and asks both providers for evidence, without drawing conclusions from counts alone.
lessons.reflection: When you review a provider or a plan, which questions come to you first: compliance questions or quality-of-life questions? What would it take to ask both?
lessons.action: Use the fictional case or an approved nonconfidential summary to draft two quality-of-life questions. Ask the responsible reviewer whether they belong in an existing template. Do not change a live review process or copy personal service records for this exercise.

check.question: Under 245D, restrictive procedures are prohibited when used for which purposes?
check.correct: As a substitute for adequate staffing, as a behavioral or therapeutic program, as punishment, or for staff convenience.
wrong: Only when used as punishment; other uses are allowed with a physician's order.
Only in settings that serve children.
check.feedback: The statute names four purposes: substitute for staffing, behavior program, punishment and staff convenience. Keeping all four in mind helps you spot restrictions that are described in neutral language but serve one of these purposes.

lessons.title: Recognizing prohibited procedures, including subtle ones
objectives: Identify examples of prohibited procedures listed in Minnesota Rules part 9544.0060.
Distinguish subtle deprivation practices from ordinary support.
Explain why removing equipment or requiring people to earn ordinary things is prohibited.
Draft a question to a provider that explores a possible hidden restriction without accusing.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota Rules part 9544.0060 lists actions and procedures that are prohibited when used as a substitute for adequate staffing, as a behavior program, as punishment or for staff convenience. Some are what most people picture: prone restraint, metal handcuffs or leg hobbles, painful techniques, tripping or pushing, and any action that might restrict a person's airway or breathing. The rule and statute distinguish prohibited procedures, specifically permitted actions and emergency manual restraint. The name of a procedure alone does not settle which provision applies. A prescription or plan does not create a general exemption; confirm the relevant authority through the responsible clinical and compliance roles.

Many items on the list are subtler and show up in everyday routines. The rule prohibits speaking to a person in a way that ridicules, demeans or threatens; using physical intimidation or a show of force; requiring a person to hold a certain posture; forced exercise; restricting a person's senses; and using intense sounds, lights or noxious sprays. The list addresses isolation without monitoring or when medically contraindicated. This does not mean that adding monitoring makes seclusion permissible; the broader prohibitions still apply. It prohibits using one person receiving services to discipline another. It prohibits interfering with a person's legal rights except as the statute allows.

Two items deserve special attention in plan review. First, the rule prohibits denying or restricting access to equipment and devices such as walkers, wheelchairs, hearing aids and communication boards. If temporary removal is needed to prevent injury or serious damage, the device must be returned as soon as the imminent risk has passed. Taking away a communication device is taking away a person's voice. Second, the rule prohibits depriving a person of normal goods and services or requiring them to earn those things, and it prohibits token or level programs that include a response cost or other negative punishment. A plan that says a person earns snacks, phone time or outings by behaving is a warning sign.

When a practice raises concern, address immediate safety needs and follow required reporting routes. Do not delay those duties for an informal discussion or your own investigation. Within your role, ask factual questions: what is this practice meant to achieve, what happens before the behavior, and what would the person say about it? Formal determinations of whether a violation occurred belong to DHS Licensing and the investigations process. Suspected maltreatment of a vulnerable adult or child must be reported under Minnesota's mandated reporting laws, whatever else is happening.
lessons.keyPoint: Look for restrictions on communication, ordinary goods and daily choices. Clarify the facts within your role, protect immediate safety and make required reports without waiting for an informal discussion.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Emeka, a case manager, reads a draft support plan addendum for Lina, who communicates mainly with a tablet. The plan says that when Lina throws objects, staff will put her tablet away for the rest of the day, and that she can earn it back by completing chores. The provider describes this as teaching responsibility. Lina's mother has mentioned that Lina seems withdrawn and has stopped trying to communicate in the evenings.
lessons.question: What should Emeka do next?
choices: Raise the concern with the provider and team: the tablet is a communication device that must be returned once any immediate risk passes, and earning it back is a prohibited practice. Ask what the throwing may be communicating and request a revised plan, while promptly following any required safety and maltreatment reporting routes.
Approve the plan because it does not involve physical restraint.
Suggest the provider keep the rule but shorten it to one hour.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It names the specific concerns under the rule, protects Lina's access to her voice, looks for the function of the behavior and asks for a better plan through the responsible process. Reporting duties do not wait for the provider’s explanation or a revised plan.
The rule covers far more than physical restraint. Denying a communication device and requiring a person to earn it back are both listed prohibited practices.
Shortening the time does not solve the problem. The practice still denies Lina her communication device beyond any immediate risk and still makes access conditional on behavior.
lessons.reflection: Think of a routine in a service setting you know that could quietly limit someone's choices. What might it look like from the person's point of view?
lessons.action: Review the fictional plan for words such as earn, privilege, lose, removed and until. Explain the concern, what remains unknown and which role should respond. An actual safety or maltreatment concern follows the required process; do not investigate it through this learning activity.

check.question: Under Minnesota Rules part 9544.0060, what must happen when a person's walker, hearing aid or communication board is temporarily removed to prevent injury or serious damage?
check.correct: It must be returned as soon as the imminent risk of injury or serious damage has passed.
wrong: It may be withheld until the person completes a behavior plan goal.
It may be withheld for up to twenty-four hours with a supervisor's approval.
check.feedback: The rule allows only temporary removal to prevent injury or serious damage and requires return as soon as that risk passes. Using the device as a reward or holding it for a set period turns it into a prohibited deprivation.

lessons.title: Emergency use of manual restraint and reporting
objectives: Explain the two conditions that must both be met for emergency use of manual restraint under 245D.
Describe the reporting and review sequence that follows an emergency use.
Identify events that providers must report on the behavior intervention report form.
Plan how oversight staff can use reports to improve a person's supports.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota Statutes section 245D.061 sets two conditions for emergency manual restraint. Immediate intervention must be needed to protect the person or others from imminent physical harm. The type used must be the least restrictive intervention that will remove that immediate risk and achieve safety. Both conditions must be met. The restraint must end when the threat of harm ends. Staff must monitor the person’s health and welfare throughout. When possible, the monitor must be someone other than the staff member implementing the restraint. An approved monitoring form is required for each incident. Providers must have a written policy, and staff must be trained before they may use emergency manual restraint. A provider may choose not to allow it and must describe the alternatives staff will use. This overview is not training in restraint techniques and does not authorize a learner to apply them.

Reporting begins before the later reviews. Section 245D.06, subdivision 1(h), requires verbal notice within twenty-four hours to the recipients specified in paragraph (b), generally the legal representative or designated emergency contact and case manager. Other incident and maltreatment reporting duties also apply. The later written-review sequence does not replace or delay them.

Within three calendar days, the staff member who implemented the restraint reports in writing to the designated coordinator. The report includes less restrictive steps tried and their duration, the person’s condition, any injuries and information about a debriefing. Use the statute’s full required list and the approved form. Within five working days of the restraint, the provider completes an internal review. It examines supports, compliance with policies, whether those policies were adequate, training needs and corrective action. Any corrective action plan required by that review must be implemented within thirty days after the review. Within five working days after that, the provider consults the expanded support team to identify what led to the behavior, what function it may have served and whether the plan should change. Within five working days of that review, the provider sends the report, internal review, any required corrective action plan and team summary to DHS and the Office of the Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities.

The Positive Supports Rule also requires providers to use the DHS behavior intervention report form for several events, including every emergency use of manual restraint, specified emergencies following a restrictive intervention, behavioral incidents leading to a 911 call and incidents requiring mobile crisis services. The list also includes crisis respite linked to a restrictive intervention and events required by a transition plan. It includes as-needed medication used to intervene in a behavioral situation, with an express exception for the prescribed treatment described in the rule. Consult the full reporting criteria and current form; this summary is not a substitute for them. Under part 9544.0070, three emergency uses of manual restraint within ninety days, or four within one hundred eighty days, trigger a positive support transition plan.

For case managers and oversight staff, these reports are information about a person's life. Repeated reports warrant review of the environment, staffing, health and support plan. They do not identify a cause by themselves. Authorized reviewers should examine the person’s account and other evidence, protect private records and identify what needs further assessment.
lessons.keyPoint: Emergency manual restraint is allowed only for imminent risk of physical harm, only in the least restrictive form and only until the threat ends. Each use triggers written reports and reviews, and repeated use triggers a positive support transition plan.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Priya is a county case manager for Deshawn, who lives in a 245D licensed home. Over six weeks she receives three behavior intervention reports describing emergency manual restraint during evening shift changes. Each report lists slightly different staff, and the internal reviews say policies were followed. No one has mentioned a positive support transition plan, and Deshawn has told Priya he hates it when new staff come in without saying who they are.
lessons.question: What should Priya do next?
choices: File the reports because the provider says policies were followed.

Ask the provider whether a positive support transition plan is now required, share the pattern she sees at shift changes and what Deshawn has told her, and request an expanded support team meeting that includes him.
Ask the provider to stop reporting unless an injury occurs, to reduce paperwork.
feedback: Policies being followed does not mean supports are working. Three emergency restraints within ninety days meets the threshold for a positive support transition plan, and the pattern needs attention.

This is the strongest response. It applies the ninety-day threshold, identifies a pattern for assessment without treating it as a proven cause, adds Deshawn's own words and uses the team process the statute requires.
Reporting is required for every emergency use of manual restraint, not only when someone is hurt. Suggesting less reporting would undermine the safeguards the law puts in place.
lessons.reflection: When a report arrives in your queue, what do you usually do with it? What would it look like to read it as a message about someone's day?
lessons.action: Use the fictional case to map the reporting and review deadlines and identify the repeated-use threshold. List questions about the shift-change pattern without deciding its cause. Do not retrieve or copy someone’s incident records solely for this exercise; actual reviews require role-based access and the designated process.

check.question: Under Minnesota Rules part 9544.0070, when must a license holder develop a positive support transition plan?
check.correct: After three incidents of emergency use of manual restraint within ninety days or four within one hundred eighty days.
wrong: After any single emergency use of manual restraint.
Only when a person is injured during a restraint.
check.feedback: The rule sets a frequency threshold: three within ninety days or four within one hundred eighty days. Every single emergency use still requires reports and reviews under 245D.061, and injury is not the trigger.

lessons.title: Transition plans and person-centered positive behavior support
objectives: Describe the timelines for a positive support transition plan under 245D.
Explain how functional behavior assessment and positive behavior support shape a good plan.
Identify the role of the External Program Review Committee.
Plan quality-of-life measures to track alongside behavior data.
lessons.teaching:
A positive support transition plan is the tool 245D uses to phase out restrictive practices safely. License holders must develop one, on DHS forms, for a person who requires intervention to maintain safety when it is known the person's behavior poses an immediate risk of physical harm to self or others. For covered admissions on or after January 1, 2014, the plan must be developed and implemented within thirty calendar days of service initiation. Prohibited interventions must be phased out no later than eleven months after plan implementation. These timelines apply to people who meet the stated conditions. The repeated-use thresholds in part 9544.0070 also require a plan. If a threshold is reached after service initiation, confirm the applicable current forms and instructions with DHS rather than restarting the service-start clock. A transition plan is not blanket permission to use prohibited practices.

The External Program Review Committee, set up under part 9544.0130, includes an expert in positive supports, a mental health professional, a licensed health professional and a representative of the Department of Health. It monitors how the rule is implemented, reviews requests for emergency use of procedures and requests to temporarily use a prohibited procedure, reviews emergency manual restraint reports and gives guidance to license holders. The committee makes recommendations; the commissioner determines requests within the applicable authority. Temporary requests have specific conditions and documentation requirements. Needing more time or submitting a request is not approval. DHS states that it will not grant a permanent variance to allow a prohibited procedure.

The content of a plan matters as much as the timeline. The rule calls for person-centered planning and functional behavior assessment. That assessment examines events before and after behavior and its possible functions. It also considers relevant health, communication and environmental factors. Qualified assessment tests explanations; it does not infer a single purpose from a brief observation or diagnosis. Positive Supports Minnesota describes an approach based on research and the person’s goals. It seeks to improve quality of life and reduce challenging behavior through changes in social interactions and settings. It also teaches communication and social skills while attending to the person’s cultural context. A good plan changes the environment and the support around the person and teaches new ways to meet the same need. It does not only describe what staff will do when things go wrong.

Quality of life belongs alongside safety, rights and required compliance measures. Alongside counts of incidents, track things the person cares about: time spent in activities they chose, relationships, sleep, health, work or school, and how often they say no and are listened to. If incidents fall while the person loses valued activities or choices, examine that tradeoff instead of declaring success from the count. Use authorized information and the person’s own priorities rather than collecting sensitive data for a learning exercise.
lessons.keyPoint: Confirm which transition-plan requirement and timeline apply. Plans need person-centered assessment and quality-of-life goals, and any temporary exception requires the applicable approval; a plan or request alone does not authorize a prohibited practice.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Bao, a DSD policy analyst, is helping a lead agency review transition plans. One plan for Yusuf includes detailed data on incidents and a clear list of staff responses, but says nothing about what Yusuf likes, what the behavior may be communicating, or what skills he will learn. The plan is on track to meet the eleven-month timeline. The team asks Bao whether the plan is acceptable because it meets every deadline.
lessons.question: What should Bao advise?
choices: Approve the plan because it meets the timeline and the data are thorough.
Recommend adding restrictions to guarantee the incident count keeps falling.

Say the timeline is only part of the picture, and recommend adding a functional behavior assessment summary, strategies that teach Yusuf new ways to meet his needs, and quality-of-life measures he helps choose.
feedback: Meeting deadlines is necessary but not enough. Without an understanding of what the behavior is for and a plan to build skills and improve Yusuf's life, restrictions may simply return later.
Adding restrictions runs directly against the purpose of the plan, which is to phase restrictive practices out, and it risks introducing prohibited procedures.
This is the strongest response. It keeps the timeline, adds the person-centered and functional elements the rule expects and measures success by Yusuf's quality of life.
lessons.reflection: What would you want a support team to track if they were measuring whether your own life was going well?
lessons.action: For the fictional case, propose two measures Yusuf could help choose and explain what you would need to ask him. Treat those as questions for the authorized team, not assumptions about his goals or instructions to collect new personal data.

check.question: What does functional behavior assessment mainly try to understand?
check.correct: What happens before a behavior and what purpose the behavior serves for the person, so supports can meet that need in a better way.
wrong: Which restrictive procedure will stop the behavior fastest.
Whether the person's diagnosis explains the behavior so no changes are needed.
check.feedback: Functional behavior assessment looks for the triggers and purpose of a behavior. That understanding lets a team change the environment and teach new skills, which is the heart of positive behavior support. It is not a way to choose a restriction or to infer its function from a diagnosis.

cards.back: Minnesota Rules chapter 9544, governing positive support strategies and restrictive interventions in 245D services and certain 245A licensed settings for people with developmental disabilities or related conditions.
Restrictive procedures may not be used as a substitute for adequate staffing, as a behavior program, as punishment or for staff convenience.

Emergency manual restraint has strict conditions, provider policy, monitoring and training requirements. It ends when the imminent threat ends and triggers notice, reporting and review. This course does not teach or authorize the technique.

A required DHS-form plan for specified safety needs or repeated emergency-restraint use. The statute gives service-start timelines for covered admissions; confirm how current instructions apply to later triggers. A plan is not blanket permission.
A qualified assessment of behavior in context, including events before and after it and possible functions, used to develop and evaluate positive supports.

aid.heading: Plan review: look for hidden restrictions
items: Words like earn, lose, privilege, removed or until attached to ordinary goods, activities or equipment.
Removal of communication devices, mobility aids or hearing aids beyond immediate risk.
Token or level systems that take away points or privileges.
Isolation or seclusion; monitoring alone does not make a prohibited practice permissible.
Any practice that could be a substitute for staffing, a behavior program, punishment or staff convenience.

aid.heading: After an emergency manual restraint
items: Verbal notice within twenty-four hours under 245D.06, subdivision 1(h), to the recipients in paragraph (b); other incident and maltreatment reports may also be required.
Written staff report to the designated coordinator within three calendar days.
Provider internal review within five working days of the emergency use.
Expanded support team review within five working days after the internal review.
Submission to DHS and the Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities within five working days after the team review.
Positive support transition plan if there are three uses in ninety days or four in one hundred eighty days.
Implement any required corrective action plan within thirty days after the internal review; confirm the current forms and complete applicable requirements.

aid.heading: Quality of life check
items: How often did the person choose their own activities this month?
How much time did they spend in the community and with people they like?
What new skills are they learning to meet the needs behind the behavior?
When they said no, were they listened to?

aid.heading: Route it correctly
items: Suspected maltreatment: report through Minnesota's mandated reporting channels right away.
Licensing compliance questions: DHS Licensing.
Temporary procedure or variance requests: follow the specific DHS process; committee review is not commissioner approval.
Plan content and supports: the person and their expanded support team.
